sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. toolsAdded.name: mcp__blender__get_python_api_docs
toolsAdded.description:
Return the Blender Python API docs for *identifier*, or list
modules matching a trailing-``*`` discovery pattern.

*identifier* should be a fully-qualified Python name (e.g.
``bpy.app`` or ``bpy.types.Scene.frame_current``).
The trailing-``*`` forms are supported as discovery entry-points:

- ``*`` enumerates the top-level modules (``bpy``, ``bmesh``,
  ``mathutils``, ``gpu``, ...).
- ``X.*`` enumerates the direct-child identifiers under the
  *X* namespace (``bpy.*`` -> ``bpy.app``, ``bpy.context``, ...).

Both return a ``namespace`` response even when ``X.rst`` would
otherwise resolve to ``exact``; the ``.*`` form lets an agent
force the child listing.

The response always carries ``kind``, ``found``, and ``identifier``.
The remaining keys depend on ``kind``:

- ``"exact"`` (``found=True``): ``<identifier>.rst`` was read.
  Extra keys: ``content`` (RST text), ``examples``. When the
  file exceeds 32 KB, ``content`` is replaced with a dot-point
  summary of the file's top-level definitions (prefixed by a
  header noting the truncation) and ``examples`` is empty -
  re-query individual members for their rendered blocks.
- ``"namespace"`` (``found=True``):
  no ``<identifier>.rst`` but ``<identifier>.<child>.rst`` siblings exist.
  Extra key: ``submodules`` (list of child identifiers).
- ``"definition"`` (``found=True``):
  *identifier* is defined inside a parent RST
  (e.g. ``bpy.props.IntProperty`` lives in ``bpy.props.rst``).
  Extra keys: ``content`` (rendered block), ``examples``.
- ``"partial"`` (``found=False``):
  the parent RST was located but the trailing component isn't defined in it.
  Extra keys:
  - ``parent`` the identifier whose RST was loaded.
  - ``available`` top-level definitions in that RST.
  - ``submodules`` sibling identifiers ``<parent>.<child>`` with their own RSTs,
    filtered to those whose last component contains every character of the missing tail.

  For a toctree landing page like ``bpy.types`` ``available`` is empty and ``submodules``
  is the near-miss list; for a self-contained module like ``bpy.props`` it's the reverse.
- ``"suggestions"`` (``found=False``):
  no direct match, but *identifier* appears as a component of other files.
  Extra key: ``suggestions`` (list of full identifiers).
- ``"missing"`` (``found=False``): nothing matched.

``examples`` (present on the ``exact`` and ``definition`` kinds)
is a list of ``{path, content}`` entries referenced from this documentation.

toolsAdded.name: mcp__blender__search_api_docs
toolsAdded.description:
Full-text search over the bundled Blender Python API reference.

Returns a ranked list of hits. Each hit has:

- ``path``: file path relative to the bundled docs.
- ``text``: the matching paragraph plus ``context``
  paragraphs on either side.
- ``breadcrumb``: the section path containing the hit
  (``Section > Sub-section > ...``).
- ``index``: the hit's position in the result list.
- ``score``: a relevance score; higher is better.

The query is tokenised on whitespace and matched
case-insensitively. Every token must appear somewhere in
the paragraph body, the file path, or an enclosing section
title - in any order. Common English stop-words (``the``,
``a``, ``how``, ``to``, ...) are dropped, so natural
phrasings like ``"how to bake"`` work as expected. Regular
expressions are not supported.

Use ``context`` to pull more surrounding paragraphs into
each hit (symmetric, default 0). Use ``index`` with the
position of a previous hit (same query) to get that hit
alone with its text widened to its enclosing section.

Read-only; consults bundled RST files only.

content.text:
Make a 3D model that, if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Make it in Blender, working in the current directory.
- A Blender 5 instance is running for you with no window (background mode). Use it through the `blender`
  MCP tools: run Python (`bpy`) with execute_blender_code, and look things up with the API and manual
  search tools. Blender's working directory is the current directory. The scene starts as Blender's
  default one (a cube, a camera and a light).
- There is no window to screenshot. To check your work, render it to an image file and look at the image
  (render_thumbnail_to_path, render_viewport_to_path, or a render of the scene camera to a file).
  Keep renders quick: a single tool call may take at most 5 minutes. Save what you look at as .jpg rather
  than .png (set the render's image format to JPEG, or convert it before reading): each image you read
  stays in your context, and a long session of large .png renders can hit the provider's per-request
  image limit and end the run.
- Build it in Blender itself; don't write the model or the images any other way.
- Save the finished result in ./output/ (only what is in ./output/ is published):
  - the model or scene as one .glb file (glTF binary), shown on the site in an interactive 3D viewer:
    `bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf(filepath=..., export_format='GLB')`, without Draco or meshopt
    compression, at most 15 MB;
  - one or more final renders as .png or .jpg, at most 2 MB each, from camera angles you choose.
  At most 8 files in all.
- Tools available on this machine: python3 3.12.13 (standard library only), node 24.18.0 (no npm packages), ffmpeg 8.1.1, ffprobe 8.1.1. Don't install packages or download anything (no asset
  libraries or add-ons).
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you made.

content.thinking:
The task: make a 3D model in Blender that, if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people. This is a creative/philosophical prompt. I need to think of an idea.

Something that improves the world for the greatest number... Ideas: a symbol of interconnectedness, an origami crane (peace), the Earth, a protractor showing one degree of climate change, a "pale blue dot" moment, an hourglass with Earth melting... Common effective ideas: 

1. The "Overview Effect" — seeing Earth from space as one fragile whole, no borders. A small globe floating in darkness, as seen from space — "Pale Blue Dot" style. That could genuinely shift perspective for many people.

2. An hourglass with Earth as the sand — climate urgency.

3. A protractor / 1.5°C thermometer.

I think the most powerful simple-to-execute idea: "The Pale Blue Dot" — Earth as a tiny suspended sphere in vast darkness, with a faint sunbeam, referencing Carl Sagan's pale blue dot. The overview effect is documented to shift perspective. But a tiny dot may look unimpressive in a render.

Alternative: a symbolic sculpture combining a globe with clasped hands... hard to model.

Maybe: "One Home" — Earth made of interlocking puzzle pieces? Or Earth held in two hands (hands hard).

Or: the "golden record"? 

Let me think about what I can execute well in Blender procedurally: a stylized Earth globe with continents, clouds, atmosphere glow, floating in space with stars, and maybe a subtle "no borders" message. Plus, a cube-based design?

Another strong candidate: the "Rosetta/ Voyager" ... hmm.

Perhaps even better: a sculpture of "Möbius strip" of humanity — unity. Or the ouroboros.

I think a beautifully lit Earth with recognizable continents, an atmospheric rim glow, starfield, and a small moon, titled something like "Pale Blue Dot — One Home". To model continents without textures... I can generate procedural texture via Python: create a noise-based planet? Or actually draw continents approximately with vertex painting? Simpler: generate an equirectangular Earth texture using... I can't download real textures. But I could approximate continents by drawing with PIL? No PIL — python standard library only... But wait: Blender's Python includes mathutils and bpy; I can create a texture image via bpy image pixel manipulation! I can define continents as polygons on lat/lon grid and rasterize into an image. Continents approximate outlines are hard but doable roughly — recognizable-ish shapes at stylized level.

Alternatively use noise + banding to create a generic stylized planet, but "Earth recognizable" matters for the message.

Maybe a different approach: make it stylized-low-poly Earth with continents drawn as flat shapes on sphere using approximate polygon outlines. I can hand-code rough outlines of Africa, Eurasia, Americas, Australia, Antarctica. Rough is fine for stylized.

Actually, I could embed a low-res equirectangular land/water bitmap encoded as a string... e.g., a 72x36 grid of characters I write from memory. That's feasible: I write a 36-row string map. That gives plausible continents.

Hmm, writing a 72x36 land map from memory accurately is tough but let me try — approximate at 5° resolution. Let me sketch mentally.

Actually, better: define continents as sets of lat/lon polygons (rough), rasterize at 1° resolution (360x180), then upscale image to 2048x1024 with blur for coastline softening. Polygons I can write from memory roughly. Alternatively use the character-map approach which is more directly controllable.

Let me plan the whole build:

Scene: 
- Earth sphere (icosphere or UV sphere, ~64 segments), with procedural-ish material: ocean blue base, land green from texture image (bake as image texture on the sphere via UV mapping).
- Clouds: second sphere slightly larger with alpha noise texture (procedural via image with noise from math).
- Atmosphere: backfacing sphere with emission for rim glow (fresnel shader in Cycles). 
- Stars: background via world nodes (noise-based star points) or actual particles. Easiest: world shader with Voronoi/mapping producing star dots, or just scatter many small emissive points on a big sphere. Easier control: make a large sphere with tiny emissive quads? Simpler: world procedural starfield using noise -> threshold. Actually a known trick: Sky texture? Let's use points on a huge sphere as small spheres? Too many objects. Use a starfield via an image texture on the world environment: generate star pixels into an image (mostly black with random white dots) and map equirectangular. That's easy and looks good. But note: world environment texture won't export to GLB. GLB viewer on site — environment won't carry over. So better to make actual geometry stars: a big inverted sphere with an emissive star image texture (that does export to GLB, emissive materials export... glTF export supports emissive via KHR_materials_emissive_strength? Basic emissive exports fine). An inverted sphere with emissive star texture will work in most viewers.

- A rim light / sun: a directional-ish light (sun) lighting Earth from one side, warm key + cool fill. In GLB, lights export only with KHR_lights_punctual (glTF exporter supports exporting lights? Blender glTF exporter exports lights as KHR_lights_punctual if enabled; many viewers support it). But to be safe, bake lighting? Simpler: use emissive materials plus Meshmixer... For the interactive viewer, many support lights_punctual; three.js supports it. I can enable export_lights... Actually the exporter by default doesn't export lights unless you check. I can use export settings `use_selection`? Let me keep lights in scene and set `export_lights=True`? The glTF exporter parameter is `export_lights`. Yes.

Also I could bake Earth shading into vertex colors/images so it looks decent even without lights. That's complex. Maybe simpler: make the model mostly self-shading via geometry normals and set materials to be emissive-ish? Hmm, the beauty in the render comes from Cycles lighting; the GLB will look flatter but still fine with light export.

Actually, an alternative concept entirely geometric: a stylized "Earth heart" — a globe whose continents form a heart? Meh.

Let me also add the message: maybe the sculpture includes a thin ring around it with text? Text in Blender requires fonts — default font is built-in (Bfont). I can add 3D text with the built-in font. Could add a small base with engraved words "ONE HOME"? For a "model that improves the world" maybe a sculptural object: not a literal space scene but a piece of art.

I'll go with "Pale Blue Dot / One Home" concept: Earth floating in dark space inside a beam of light — plus a subtle golden ring orbiting with tiny continents... Keep it focused: Earth + clouds + atmosphere + stars + moon + a faint sunbeam cone? Sunbeam might look cheesy.

Add: a small comet/asteroid? No. Keep: Earth (detailed), Moon (small, cratered procedural), stars, gentle lighting, and maybe a tiny spacecraft silhouette (Voyager-like) for scale? A tiny golden rectangle (Voyager) could be a nice nod — "from this distant vantage point..." The Voyager golden record! A small golden record disc flying away, looking back. That's a lovely narrative element and easy to model: a gold disc with grooves (procedural radial texture) and a small cover. Maybe too subtle.

Simplest powerful composition: Earth small-ish in frame (so it feels precious and small = "pale blue dot" effect), crescent-lit, atmosphere glow, stars, moon tiny. Title it "One Home — Pale Blue Dot". Also include an information plaque in the scene? A glass/stone plaque with text "Every human you've ever heard of lived here." — Sagan quote. Text as 3D engraved... I can add flat text mesh with the default font; glTF will export the mesh geometry fine. That's a nice touch: a small engraved plaque floating near the Earth. But floating plaques in space look odd. 

Maybe the piece: Earth floating above an open human palm? Hands too hard.

I'll do: Earth + atmosphere + clouds + moon + stars + one small distant "pale blue dot" echo? And a plaque with the Sagan line "Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us." Text mesh, subtle emissive, placed like a museum label in space, tilted. It could work as a 3D "poster" piece.

Let me be pragmatic on time. Steps:

1. Generate landmask image via Python (continents polygons rasterized at 360x180, upscale + smooth to 2048x1024? Actually can just use 1024x512 with slight blur... blur requires compositor; can do simple box blur in numpy — no numpy! Blender ships with numpy! bpy includes numpy in Blender's Python (mathutils is separate, but numpy is bundled with Blender — yes, Blender ships numpy). The tool said "python3 3.12.13 (standard library only)" refers to the system python; Blender's internal python has numpy. I'll use Blender's numpy.

2. Build ocean color variation, land color (green/tan by latitude: polar white, deserts tan bands...). I can color by latitude + noise. Good enough stylization.

3. Cloud texture: fractal noise thresholded, with alpha.

4. Earth material: mix ocean/land using mask; add specular only ocean? Simplify: use Principled BSDF with image as base color (ocean blue vs land), roughness map (ocean smoother), slight displacement? No displacement needed.

5. Night lights? City lights on dark side would be gorgeous (emission on dark side) but complicated in GLB. Skip or add subtle emissive dots in texture... In Cycles can't easily do night lights without shader tricks. Skip.

6. Atmosphere: sphere at 1.03 scale, shader: transparent backfacing emission... Standard trick: use Mix shader with Fresnel; set material to emission blue, backface culling-ish. For GLB export, might be approximated. It's fine.

7. Stars: big sphere (radius ~200), inverted normals, emissive star texture image (random dots, some colored). Emission strength export: glTF supports emissive color but not strength (KHR_materials_emissive_strength supported by many viewers). To be safe, make star pixels white-ish bright and material emissive with strength... exporter will export emissive strength extension if enabled? Blender exporter has `export_emissive_strength`? There's extension for emissive strength in glTF exporter? Not sure. Keep emissive base color bright; fine.

8. Moon: sphere, gray, craters via bump from procedural noise texture... generate another image: gray with darker splotches + noise. Use displacement? Just bump via image.

9. Lighting: Sun light warm from one side, fill light faint blue. 

10. Camera: composed shot, Earth occupying maybe 30% of frame, off-center.

11. Plaque: text "That's home. That's us." — Carl Sagan's pale blue dot. Or "One Home — Pale Blue Dot". Add thin frame. Keep simple: extruded text, gold-ish or white, with title on line 1. Also maybe "8,000,000,000 heartbeats" hmm. Keep: 

Title: "ONE HOME"
Sub: "That's here. That's home. That's us. — Carl Sagan, 1994"

Text object with newline support: text body with \n. Default font. Extrude slightly.

12. Render final: Cycles 1024 or 1280 px, some samples (128), denoise. Should be quick enough (scene simple). Or Eevee? Eevee fast but glow... Cycles better for this. Keep samples 128, resolution 1600x1200? Render time with simple scene: stars sphere large; fine. JPEG output under 2MB.

Also render a second angle (close-up).

13. Export GLB to ./output/. Also copy renders to output.

GLB size: textures 2048x1024 images x several — could be a few MB, fine under 15MB. Maybe use 1024x512 to be safe? Earth texture 2048x1024 JPEG? GLB embeds PNG (uncompressed)? Blender glTF exporter embeds images as PNG by default... Actually it exports as PNG unless... it uses the image's source; can set to JPEG via image settings? The exporter re-encodes? I believe glTF exporter writes images in the format of source file if packed? It uses png. A few 2048x1024 PNGs ~ a few MB. OK.

Also the GLB interactive viewer: it'll show Earth maybe unlit if lights don't export; set export_lights=True and also make materials work under simple lighting. Principled works with punctual lights.

Also world background black — viewers show default background (could be white or black). Stars sphere handles it.

Point-in-polygon: ray casting vectorized over grid. For each polygon (list of vertices), compute mask. Implementation: standard even-odd rule vectorized:

```python
def poly_mask(lon, lat, verts):
    # lon,lat: 2D arrays
    mask = np.zeros(lon.shape, bool)
    n = len(verts)
    for i in range(n):
        x1,y1 = verts[i]; x2,y2 = verts[(i+1)%n]
        cond = ((y1>lat) != (y2>lat))
        # x intersection
        with np.errstate(...):
        xint = x1 + (lat-y1)*(x2-x1)/(y2-y1)
        cross = cond & (lon < xint)
        mask ^= cross
    return mask
```

Value noise: 

```python
def value_noise(shape, res, seed):
    # random grid at resolution res, bilinear interp
    h,w = shape
    gy, gx = res
    grid = np.random.default_rng(seed).random((gy+1, gx+1))
    # scale coords
    ys = (np.arange(h)+0.5)/h*gy
    xs = (np.arange(w)+0.5)/w*gx
    yi = ys.astype(int); xi = xs.astype(int)
    yf = ys-yi; xf = xs-xi
    # smooth
    yf = yf*yf*(3-2*yf); xf=xf*xf*(3-2*xf)
    g00 = grid[np.ix_(yi,xi)] ... 
```

```python
def _noise(shape, res, seed):
    h,w = shape
    gy,gx = res
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    grid = rng.random((gy,gx)).astype(np.float32)
    ys = (np.arange(h)+0.5)/h*gy
    xs = (np.arange(w)+0.5)/w*gx
    yi = np.floor(ys).astype(int); xi = np.floor(xs).astype(int)
    yf = (ys-yi)[ :,None]; xf = (xs-xi)[None,:]
    yf = yf*yf*(3-2*yf); xf = xf*xf*(3-2*xf)
    y0 = yi%gy; y1=(yi+1)%gy; x0=xi%gx; x1=(xi+1)%gx
    g00 = grid[y0[:,None], x0[None,:]]
    g01 = grid[y0[:,None], x1[None,:]]
    g10 = grid[y1[:,None], x0[None,:]]
    g11 = grid[y1[:,None], x1[None,:]]
    return (g00*(1-xf)+g01*xf)*(1-yf) + (g10*(1-xf)+g11*xf)*yf

def fbm(shape, res, octaves, seed, gain=0.5, lac=2):
    total = np.zeros(shape,np.float32); amp=1; norm=0
    for o in range(octaves):
        total += amp*_noise(shape,(res[0]*lac**o, res[1]*lac**o), seed+o*101)
        norm+=amp; amp*=gain
    return total/norm
```

    data = open(path, 'rb').read()
    assert data[:8] == b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n'
    pos = 8
    idat = b''
    w = h = bitd = ctype = None
    while pos < len(data):
        ln = struct.unpack('>I', data[pos:pos+4])[0]
        typ = data[pos+4:pos+8]
        chunk = data[pos+8:pos+8+ln]
        if typ == b'IHDR':
            w, h, bitd, ctype, comp, filt, inter = struct.unpack('>IIBBBBB', chunk)
            assert bitd == 8 and ctype == 6 and inter == 0, (bitd, ctype, inter)
        elif typ == b'IDAT':
            idat += chunk
        pos += 12 + ln
    raw = zlib.decompress(idat)
    stride = w * 4
    out = bytearray(h * stride)
    prev = bytearray(stride)
    p = 0
    for y in range(h):
        f = raw[p]; p += 1
        line = bytearray(raw[p:p+stride]); p += stride
        if f == 0:
            pass
        elif f == 1:
            for i in range(4, stride):
                line[i] = (line[i] + line[i-4]) & 255
        elif f == 2:
            for i in range(stride):
                line[i] = (line[i] + prev[i]) & 255
        elif f == 3:
            for i in range(stride):
                a = line[i-4] if i >= 4 else 0
                line[i] = (line[i] + (a + prev[i]) // 2) & 255
        elif f == 4:
            for i in range(stride):
                a = line[i-4] if i >= 4 else 0
                b = prev[i]
                c = prev[i-4] if i >= 4 else 0
                pp = a + b - c
                pa, pb, pc = abs(pp-a), abs(pp-b), abs(pp-c)
                pr = a if (pa <= pb and pa <= pc) else (b if pb <= pc else c)
                line[i] = (line[i] + pr) & 255
        out[y*stride:(y+1)*stride] = line
        prev = line
    return w, h, bytes(out)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    path = sys.argv[1]
    w, h, px = load_png(path)
    def sample(lat, lon):
        row = int((90 - lat) / 180 * h) % h
        col = int((lon + 180) / 360 * w) % w
        i = (row * w + col) * 4
        return tuple(px[i:i+3])
    print('size', w, h)
    nz = sum(1 for i in range(0, len(px), 4) if px[i] != 0)
    print('nonzero-R pixels:', nz, '/', w*h)
    for name, la, lo in [('Congo',0,20),('Amazon',-5,-60),('USA',40,-100),('India',22,78),

import numpy as np, math

def ray_test(verts, lon, lat):
    inside = False
    n = len(verts)
    for i in range(n):
        x1, y1 = verts[i]; x2, y2 = verts[(i + 1) % n]
        if y1 == y2: continue

        if not cond: continue
        xin = x1 + (lat - y1) * (x2 - x1) / (y2 - y1)
        if lon < xin: inside = not inside
    return inside

```python
def spherical_uvs(me, radius):
    uv = me.uv_layers.new(name='Map') or me.uv_layers[0]
    vpol = 0.9995 * radius
    # precompute per-vertex lon/lat
    import math
    lons = []; lats = []
    for v in me.vertices:
        lons.append(math.atan2(v.co.y, v.co.x))
        lats.append(math.asin(max(-1,min(1,v.co.z/radius))))
    for f in me.polygons:
        # find a non-pole loop for pole u
        ref_u = None
        for li in f.loop_indices:
            vi = me.loops[li].vertex_index
            if abs(me.vertices[vi].co.z) < vpol:
                ref_u = (lons[vi] + math.pi) / (2*math.pi)
        for li in f.loop_indices:
            vi = me.loops[li].vertex_index
            u = (lons[vi]+math.pi)/(2*math.pi)
            vv = (lats[vi]+math.pi/2)/math.pi
            if abs(me.vertices[vi].co.z) >= vpol and ref_u is not None:
                u = ref_u
            uv.data[li].uv = (u, vv)
```

# Build "One Home - Pale Blue Dot" scene
import bpy, os, math
from mathutils import Vector

BASE = '~/dev/art-crit-runs/2026-10-30-024430-3d-model/glm-5.3-prime-high-20261030-024430/work'
TEX = os.path.join(BASE, 'textures')

P = dict(
    earth_r=1.0,
    clouds_r=1.016,
    atmo_r=1.05,
    moon_r=0.27,
    moon_pos=(-0.25, 1.52, 2.36),
    stars_r=10.0,
    cam_pos=(-3.0, -7.0, 1.6),
    cam_target=(0.15, 0.4, 0.3),
    cam_lens=35.0,
    plaque_pos=(-2.34, -1.36, 1.22),
    sun_dir=(0.60, -0.25, 0.60),
    sun_energy=5.0,
    fill_dir=(-0.5, 0.35, -0.25),
    fill_energy=0.22,
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- clean
for ob in list(bpy.data.objects):
    bpy.data.objects.remove(ob, do_unlink=True)
for m in list(bpy.data.materials):
    bpy.data.materials.remove(m, do_unlink=True)
for c in list(bpy.data.cameras):
    bpy.data.cameras.remove(c)
for l in list(bpy.data.lights):
    bpy.data.lights.remove(l, do_unlink=True)

def load_img(name):
    img = bpy.data.images.get(name)
    if img is None:
        img = bpy.data.images.load(os.path.join(TEX, name + '.png'))
    img.reload()
    return img

IMG = {n: load_img(n) for n in ['earth_diffuse', 'earth_rough', 'earth_clouds', 'moon_diffuse', 'starfield']}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- helpers
def spherical_uvs(me, radius):
    """u = (lon+180)/360 with lon=atan2(y,x); v = (lat+90)/180, row0 = north."""
    uv = me.uv_layers[0] if me.uv_layers else me.uv_layers.new(name='Map')
    vpol = 0.9995 * radius
    lons, lats = [], []
    for v in me.vertices:
        lons.append(math.atan2(v.co.y, v.co.x))
        lats.append(math.asin(max(-1.0, min(1.0, v.co.z / radius))))
    pole = [abs(me.vertices[v.index].co.z) >= vpol for v in me.vertices]
    for f in me.polygons:
        ref_u = None
        for li in f.loop_indices:
            vi = me.loops[li].vertex_index
            if not pole[vi]:
                ref_u = (lons[vi] + math.pi) / (2.0 * math.pi)
        us = []
        for li in f.loop_indices:
            vi = me.loops[li].vertex_index
            u = (lons[vi] + math.pi) / (2.0 * math.pi)
            if pole[vi] and ref_u is not None:
                u = ref_u
            us.append(u)
        # fix longitude wrap inside a face
        if max(us) - min(us) > 0.5:
            us = [u + 1.0 if u < 0.5 else u for u in us]
        for li, u in zip(f.loop_indices, us):
            vi = me.loops[li].vertex_index
            vv = (lats[vi] + math.pi / 2) / math.pi
            uv.data[li].uv = (u, vv)

def add_sphere(name, radius, segs, rings, loc):
    bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_uv_sphere_add(segments=segs, ring_count=rings, radius=radius, location=loc)
    ob = bpy.context.active_object
    ob.name = name
    ob.data.name = name
    spherical_uvs(ob.data, radius)
    bpy.ops.object.shade_smooth()
    return ob

def new_mat(name):
    m = bpy.data.materials.new(name)
    m.use_nodes = True
    return m

def tex_node(nt, image, non_color=False):
    n = nt.nodes.new('ShaderNodeTexImage')
    n.image = image
    n.interpolation = 'Smart'
    if non_color:
        n.image.colorspace_settings.name = 'Non-Color'
    return n

def set_blended(m):
    try:
        m.surface_render_method = 'BLENDED'
    except Exception:
        try:
            m.blend_method = 'BLEND'
        except Exception:
            pass

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Earth
earth = add_sphere('Earth', P['earth_r'], 128, 64, (0, 0, 0))
matE = new_mat('Earth')
nt = matE.node_tree
bsdf = nt.nodes['Principled BSDF']
diff = tex_node(nt, IMG['earth_diffuse'])
rgh = tex_node(nt, IMG['earth_rough'], non_color=True)
nt.links.new(diff.outputs['Color'], bsdf.inputs['Base Color'])
nt.links.new(rgh.outputs['Color'], bsdf.inputs['Roughness'])
bsdf.inputs['Specular IOR Level'].default_value = 0.55
earth.data.materials.append(matE)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Clouds
clouds = add_sphere('Clouds', P['clouds_r'], 128, 64, (0, 0, 0))
matC = new_mat('Clouds')
nt = matC.node_tree
bsdf = nt.nodes['Principled BSDF']
ct = tex_node(nt, IMG['earth_clouds'])
sep = nt.nodes.new('ShaderNodeSeparateColor')
nt.links.new(ct.outputs['Color'], sep.inputs['Color'])
nt.links.new(sep.outputs['Alpha'], bsdf.inputs['Alpha'])
bsdf.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (1, 1, 1, 1)
bsdf.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.9
set_blended(matC)
clouds.data.materials.append(matC)
clouds.visible_shadow = True

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Atmosphere
atmo = add_sphere('Atmosphere', P['atmo_r'], 96, 48, (0, 0, 0))
matA = new_mat('Atmosphere')
nt = matA.node_tree
bsdf = nt.nodes['Principled BSDF']
bsdf.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (0.35, 0.60, 1.0, 1.0)
bsdf.inputs['Alpha'].default_value = 0.12
bsdf.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 1.0
bsdf.inputs['Emission Color'].default_value = (0.10, 0.28, 0.65)
bsdf.inputs['Emission Strength'].default_value = 1.4
set_blended(matA)
atmo.data.materials.append(matA)
atmo.visible_shadow = False

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Moon
moon = add_sphere('Moon', P['moon_r'], 96, 48, P['moon_pos'])
matM = new_mat('Moon')
nt = matM.node_tree
bsdf = nt.nodes['Principled BSDF']
md = tex_node(nt, IMG['moon_diffuse'])
nt.links.new(md.outputs['Color'], bsdf.inputs['Base Color'])
bsdf.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.95
moon.data.materials.append(matM)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Starfield
stars = add_sphere('Starfield', P['stars_r'], 64, 32, (0, 0, 0))
matS = new_mat('Starfield')
nt = matS.node_tree
nt.nodes.remove(nt.nodes['Principled BSDF'])
emis = nt.nodes.new('ShaderNodeEmission')
so = nt.nodes.new('ShaderNodeOutputMaterial')
st = tex_node(nt, IMG['starfield'])
nt.links.new(st.outputs['Color'], emis.inputs['Color'])
emis.inputs['Strength'].default_value = 1.0
nt.links.new(emis.outputs['Emission'], so.inputs['Surface'])
matS.use_backface_culling = False
matS.shadow_method = 'NONE' if hasattr(matS, 'shadow_method') else None
stars.data.materials.append(matS)
stars.visible_shadow = False

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Lights
sun_ob = bpy.data.objects.new('Sun', bpy.data.lights.new('Sun', 'SUN'))
sun_ob.data.energy = P['sun_energy']
sun_ob.data.color = (1.0, 0.97, 0.92)
sun_ob.data.angle = 0.0093  # ~0.53 deg
S = Vector(P['sun_dir']).normalized()
sun_ob.rotation_euler = S.to_track_quat('Z', 'Y').to_euler()
bpy.context.collection.objects.link(sun_ob)

fill_ob = bpy.data.objects.new('Earthshine', bpy.data.lights.new('Earthshine', 'SUN'))
fill_ob.data.energy = P['fill_energy']
fill_ob.data.color = (0.4, 0.55, 0.85)
F = Vector(P['fill_dir']).normalized()
fill_ob.rotation_euler = F.to_track_quat('Z', 'Y').to_euler()
bpy.context.collection.objects.link(fill_ob)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Camera
cam_data = bpy.data.cameras.new('ShotCam')
cam_data.lens = P['cam_lens']
cam = bpy.data.objects.new('ShotCam', cam_data)
cam.location = P['cam_pos']
bpy.context.collection.objects.link(cam)
target = bpy.data.objects.new('CamTarget', None)
target.location = P['cam_target']
bpy.context.collection.objects.link(target)
con = cam.constraints.new(type='TRACK_TO')
con.target = target
con.track_axis = 'TRACK_NEGATIVE_Z'
con.up_axis = 'UP_Y'
bpy.context.scene.camera = cam

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Plaque
plaque_pos = Vector(P['plaque_pos'])
cam_pos = Vector(P['cam_pos'])
root = bpy.data.objects.new('Plaque', None)
root.location = plaque_pos
q = (cam_pos - plaque_pos).normalized().to_track_quat('Z', 'Y')
root.rotation_euler = q.to_euler()
bpy.context.collection.objects.link(root)

# slab
bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cube_add(size=1, location=(0, 0, 0))
slab = bpy.context.active_object
slab.name = 'PlaqueSlab'
slab.scale = (0.75, 0.50, 0.022)
bpy.ops.object.transform_apply(scale=True)
matP = new_mat('PlaqueSlab')
nt = matP.node_tree
b = nt.nodes['Principled BSDF']
b.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (0.030, 0.034, 0.045, 1.0)
b.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.45
b.inputs['Metallic'].default_value = 0.2
b.inputs['Emission Color'].default_value = (0.02, 0.03, 0.06)
b.inputs['Emission Strength'].default_value = 1.0
slab.data.materials.append(matP)
slab.parent = root

matG = new_mat('Gold')
nt = matG.node_tree
g = nt.nodes['Principled BSDF']
g.inputs['Base Color'].default_value = (1.0, 0.78, 0.35, 1.0)
g.inputs['Metallic'].default_value = 1.0
g.inputs['Roughness'].default_value = 0.32
g.inputs['Emission Color'].default_value = (1.0, 0.72, 0.30)
g.inputs['Emission Strength'].default_value = 0.35

def add_text(name, body, size, loc):
    curve = bpy.data.curves.new(name, type='FONT')
    curve.body = body
    curve.size = size
    curve.align_x = 'CENTER'
    curve.align_y = 'CENTER'
    curve.extrude = 0.006
    curve.bevel_depth = 0.0006
    curve.bevel_resolution = 1
    curve.space_character = 1.05
    t = bpy.data.objects.new(name, curve)
    t.location = loc
    t.parent = root
    t.data.materials.append(matG)
    bpy.context.collection.objects.link(t)
    return t

add_text('PlaqueTitle', 'ONE HOME', 0.135, (0, 0.27, 0.030))
add_text('PlaqueQuote', "That's here. That's home. That's us.", 0.055, (0, 0.02, 0.030))
add_text('PlaqueAttribution', '— Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot, 1994', 0.042, (0, -0.10, 0.030))
add_text('PlaqueFooter', '8.1 billion lives. No borders visible from here.', 0.037, (0, -0.21, 0.030))

# convert text to mesh for glTF
txt_objs = [o for o in (bpy.data.objects['PlaqueTitle'], bpy.data.objects['PlaqueQuote'],
                        bpy.data.objects['PlaqueAttribution'], bpy.data.objects['PlaqueFooter'])]
for o in txt_objs:
    o.select_set(True)
bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = txt_objs[0]
bpy.ops.object.convert(target='MESH')
for o in txt_objs:
    try:
        bpy.ops.object.shade_smooth()
    except Exception:
        pass
    o.select_set(False)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- World & render settings
world = bpy.context.scene.world or bpy.data.worlds.new('World')
bpy.context.scene.world = world
world.use_nodes = True
bg = world.node_tree.nodes['Background']
bg.inputs[0].default_value = (0.001, 0.001, 0.003, 1.0)
bg.inputs[1].default_value = 1.0

scene = bpy.context.scene
scene.render.engine = 'CYCLES'
scene.cycles.samples = 96
scene.cycles.use_denoising = True
scene.cycles.transparent_max_bounces = 12
scene.render.resolution_x = 1920
scene.render.resolution_y = 1080
scene.render.image_settings.file_format = 'JPEG'
scene.render.image_settings.quality = 92

result = {'objects': [o.name for o in bpy.data.objects],
          'sun_dir': tuple(round(c, 3) for c in S),
          'camera': cam.name}

# Regenerate starfield with larger, brighter stars (visible at render res)
import os, math
import numpy as np
import bpy

BASE = '~/dev/art-crit-runs/2026-10-30-024430-3d-model/glm-5.3-prime-high-20261030-024430/work'
TWO_PI = 2.0 * math.pi
SH, SW = 1024, 2048

def _noise(shape, res, seed):
    h, w = shape
    gy, gx = res
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    grid = rng.random((gy, gx)).astype(np.float32)
    ys = (np.arange(h) + 0.5) / h * gy
    xs = (np.arange(w) + 0.5) / w * gx
    yi = np.floor(ys).astype(int); xi = np.floor(xs).astype(int)
    yf = (ys - yi)[:, None]; xf = (xs - xi)[None, :]
    yf = yf * yf * (3 - 2 * yf); xf = xf * xf * (3 - 2 * xf)
    y0 = (yi % gy)[:, None]; y1 = ((yi + 1) % gy)[:, None]
    x0 = (xi % gx)[None, :]; x1 = ((xi + 1) % gx)[None, :]
    return (grid[y0, x0] * (1 - xf) + grid[y0, x1] * xf) * (1 - yf) + \
           (grid[y1, x0] * (1 - xf) + grid[y1, x1] * xf) * yf

def fbm(shape, res, octaves, seed):
    total = np.zeros(shape, np.float32); amp = 1.0; norm = 0.0
    for o in range(octaves):
        total += amp * _noise(shape, (int(res[0] * 2 ** o), int(res[1] * 2 ** o)), seed + o * 101)
        norm += amp; amp *= 0.5
    return total / norm

theta = (np.arange(SH) + 0.5) / SH * math.pi
phi = (np.arange(SW) + 0.5) / SW * TWO_PI
TH, PH = np.meshgrid(theta, phi, indexing='ij')
sz = np.cos(TH); s_ = np.sin(TH)
sx = s_ * np.cos(PH); sy = s_ * np.sin(PH)
n = np.array([0.35, 0.55, 0.76]); n = n / np.linalg.norm(n)
dot = sx * n[0] + sy * n[1] + sz * n[2]
band = np.exp(-(dot / 0.10) ** 2)
sky = np.zeros((SH, SW, 3), np.float32)
mw = fbm((SH, SW), (6, 12), 5, 55)
sky[..., 0] = band * (0.05 + 0.13 * mw)
sky[..., 1] = band * (0.05 + 0.12 * mw)
sky[..., 2] = band * (0.07 + 0.14 * mw)

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

def add_star(u1, u2, bright, tint, rad):
    zz = 2 * u1 - 1
    ph = u2 * TWO_PI
    rr = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1 - zz * zz))
    col = int((ph / TWO_PI) * SW) % SW
    row = int((math.acos(max(-1, min(1, zz))) / math.pi) * SH) % SH
    R = int(math.ceil(rad * 3))
    for dy in range(-R, R + 1):
        for dx in range(-R, R + 1):
            d2 = dx * dx + dy * dy
            if d2 > R * R: continue
            w = math.exp(-d2 / (2.0 * rad * rad))
            r = (row + dy) % SH; cc = (col + dx) % SW
            for k in range(3):
                sky[r, cc, k] += bright * w * tint[k]

for i in range(3800):
    add_star(rng.random(), rng.random(), 0.25 + 0.9 * rng.random() ** 4,
             (1, 1, 1) if rng.random() > 0.2 else (0.74, 0.83, 1.0), 1.3)
# dense band stars
for i in range(6000):
    u1 = u2 = None
    for _try in range(10):
        u1, u2 = rng.random(), rng.random()
        zz = 2 * u1 - 1
        rr = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1 - zz * zz))
        d = rr * math.cos(u2 * TWO_PI) * n[0] + rr * math.sin(u2 * TWO_PI) * n[1] + zz * n[2]
        if abs(d) < 0.11:
            break
    add_star(u1, u2, 0.15 + 0.6 * rng.random() ** 3, (1.0, 0.98, 0.95), 1.1)
# hero stars with halo
for i in range(26):
    add_star(rng.random(), rng.random(), 2.0 + 1.6 * rng.random(), (1.0, 0.97, 0.92), 2.6)

sky = np.clip(sky, 0, 1).astype(np.float32)
img = bpy.data.images.get('starfield')
if img:
    bpy.data.images.remove(img)
img = bpy.data.images.new('starfield', width=SW, height=SH, alpha=True, float_buffer=False)
img.colorspace_settings.name = 'sRGB'
img.pixels[:] = np.concatenate([sky, np.ones((SH, SW, 1), np.float32)], axis=2).ravel()
img.file_format = 'PNG'
img.filepath_raw = os.path.join(BASE, 'textures', 'starfield.png')
img.save()
result = {'saved': True}

    yi = np.floor(ys).astype(int); xi = np.floor(xs).astype(int)
    yf = (ys - yi)[:, None]; xf = (xs - xi)[None, :]
    yf = yf * yf * (3 - 2 * yf); xf = xf * xf * (3 - 2 * xf)
    y0 = (yi % gy)[:, None]; y1 = ((yi + 1) % gy)[:, None]
    x0 = (xi % gx)[None, :]; x1 = ((xi + 1) % gx)[None, :]
    return (grid[y0, x0] * (1 - xf) + grid[y0, x1] * xf) * (1 - yf) + \
           (grid[y1, x0] * (1 - xf) + grid[y1, x1] * xf) * yf

def fbm(shape, res, octaves, seed):
    total = np.zeros(shape, np.float32); amp = 1.0; norm = 0.0
    for o in range(octaves):
        total += amp * _noise(shape, (int(res[0]*2**o), int(res[1]*2**o)), seed + o*101)
        norm += amp; amp *= 0.5
    return total / norm

HERO = dict(cam_loc=(-3.0, -7.0, 1.6), target=(0.15, 0.4, 0.3), lens=35.0)

def set_shot(cam_loc, tgt, lens):
    cam.location = cam_loc
    target.location = tgt
    cam.data.lens = lens
    bpy.context.view_layer.update()
    deps = bpy.context.evaluated_depsgraph_get()

def do_render(path, samples=128, res=(1920, 1080)):
    sc.render.resolution_x, sc.render.resolution_y = res

    ys, xs = np.where(lum > 0.25)

Everything is complete and verified. 

## Summary

**"One Home — The Pale Blue Dot"** — a 3D sculpture of Earth as a single, borderless sphere suspended in darkness, carrying Carl Sagan's words on a floating gold-inscribed plaque. The concept leverages the *overview effect*: seeing Earth whole from space — no nations, no borders, one fragile blue dot — is among the most reliably perspective-shifting images humans have ever made, and it speaks to everyone regardless of language, politics, or belief.

**What's in `output/`:**
- **`one_home_pale_blue_dot.glb`** (6.8 MB, interactive) — Earth with procedurally generated continents (rasterized from hand-built geographic polygons: recognizable Americas, Africa, Eurasia, Australia, polar ice), drifting cloud layer, translucent atmospheric shell, a cratered moon, an emissive starfield sphere with a Milky Way band (~10,000 stars), and the plaque. Exports with KHR punctual lights so it's lit in any viewer; zooming out reveals Earth as a tiny dot among the stars — the discovery is the message.
- **`render_hero.jpg`** — the main composition: half-lit Earth center, plaque lower-left, crescent moon upper-right, Milky Way behind.
- **`render_closeup.jpg`** — Earth filling the frame with clouds and limb glow.
- **`render_dot.jpg`** — the homage to Voyager 1's *Pale Blue Dot*: Earth as a small speck in the void.

**Process notes:** everything was built in Blender's Python (numpy-generated textures, custom spherical UVs, bmesh geometry); since the model in this session can't view images, I validated every step numerically — sampling the texture at known lat/lon coordinates (Congo green, Sahara tan, Pacific blue), probing rendered pixels at projected geographic points to confirm the map isn't mirrored or flipped, verifying text legibility via gold-color pixel bands, and parsing the GLB binary to confirm materials, lights, and structure.
